analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-run public health plan anyone could buy, and caps out-of-pocket drug and medical costs for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would create a new government-run insurance option, 'Medicare Part E,' that any individual or employer could buy through the ACA marketplaces, covering benefits at the generous 'gold' level including abortion and reproductive services. It would also cap Medicare beneficiaries' yearly out-of-pocket costs at $6,700, let the government negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers, expand ACA premium tax credits to households earning up to six times the poverty level, put $30 billion into a fund to lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and require regulators to act against excessive insurance rates. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and marketplace shoppers gain a cheaper, more generous public plan option; employers and their workers gain a voluntary government-administered group plan; Medicare beneficiaries gain a hard annual cap on out-of-pocket costs; and anyone buying Part D drugs gains from government-negotiated prices. Low-income households gain richer subsidies and lower cost-sharing, and consumers in high-rate insurance markets gain a regulator authorized to force rate rollbacks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace shoppers, Medicare beneficiaries, drug buyers

how_it_helps.text: Creates 'Medicare Part E' public plans offered on the exchanges in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, open to any U.S. resident, with providers required to participate if they take regular Medicare.

Each public plan must cover benefits at the gold level, meaning lower deductibles and copays than typical silver plans, and must cover abortions and reproductive services even where state law would prohibit it.
Lets employers enroll in the public plan and requires CMS to serve as the plan's administrator, with portability so workers keep the plan if they lose their job.
Caps annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing for Medicare Part A and B services at $6,700 starting in 2023, adjusted for medical inflation — today traditional Medicare has no such cap.

Repeals the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices and requires the Secretary to negotiate Part D prices, falling back to the price paid by the Department of Veterans Affairs if talks fail after a year.
Expands ACA premium tax credits to households earning up to 600% of the poverty level (up from 400%) and bases the credit on the second-lowest-cost gold plan rather than the cheaper silver plan.
Appropriates $2 billion for startup costs and $30 billion for 2022-2024 for a reinsurance and affordability fund that lowers premiums and out-of-pocket costs in the individual market in every state.

Extends community-rating rules to large employer plans and gives federal or state regulators authority to correct, deny, or rebate excessive, unjustified, or discriminatory insurance rates, including for grandfathered plans.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose customers to a public competitor; brand-name drug makers would face government-negotiated prices backed by a VA-price fallback; hospitals and doctors would accept rates capped between Medicare and commercial levels; and federal taxpayers fund the startup, reserves, and the $30 billion affordability fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, drug makers, providers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Provider payment rates under the public plan would be set between Medicare's low rates and commercial rates, and providers warn lower Medicare-scale payments can force hospitals to shift costs to other payers or reduce service availability, especially rural hospitals.

The federal government would directly fund the plan's startup ($2 billion) and its initial claim reserves, and would pour $30 billion into the individual market — significant taxpayer spending that private insurers argue gives the public plan a subsidized leg up in competition.

The drug-negotiation backstop sets the price to the lower of the VA's procurement price if negotiation fails, and insurers and manufacturers objected in general to government-set prices as potentially reducing investment in new medicines — a cost borne by future patients, not just manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the biggest pain points in American health care: expensive marketplace premiums, seniors' uncapped cost-sharing, and unpunished rate hikes. The costs are real — tens of billions in new federal spending and lower revenue for insurers, drug makers, and providers — but they are the direct price of a public option and price controls, and the bill is designed to pay insurers and consumers through the same fund rather than cut anyone's existing benefits. It is an ambitious, fairly coherent affordability package, not a narrowly focused fix.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Finance Committee in April 2021, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died there when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Choose Medicare Act on April 15, 2021, joined by 11 fellow Democrats listed on the bill.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
The bill's 12 cosponsors were all Senate Democrats — 12 of 48 — and no Republican cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and brand-name drug makers are better off because the bill died: no public competitor entered the market, Medicare's drug-price noninterference ban stayed in place, and providers kept negotiating payment rates without a Medicare-scale fallback. The bill's sponsors were the main losers, along with the uninsured and Medicare beneficiaries it targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and drug makers kept the status quo

industries.note: The bill creates a direct government competitor that could take their customers in individual, small-group, and large-group markets, and extends rating and rate-review rules to more of their business. At the same time, $30 billion in reinsurance payments and gold-level subsidy benchmarks would channel federal money through their exchange plans.

The bill repeals the statutory ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices and backstops failed negotiations with the VA's price, directly cutting what Medicare pays for Part D drugs — savings that flow to beneficiaries and taxpayers out of manufacturer revenue.

Providers taking Medicare would be required into the public plan's network with rates negotiated between Medicare's low rates and commercial rates, plus limits on balance billing — lower than commercial revenue but higher than Medicare's. Their interest in higher reimbursement runs against consumers' interest in lower prices.

Employers gain a voluntary, government-administered group plan that could be cheaper than commercial coverage and must offer navigators to employees whose coverage is unaffordable — but rate-setting rules would newly apply to large-group plans.

The bill authorizes open-ended appropriations to expand the ACA navigator program and requires employers without affordable coverage to refer every full-time employee to a navigator, growing that sector's work.
